title: Finite RH verification composes witness counts with an independent total
claim: Critical-line sign changes provide a lower count of zeros with the desired location, while an argument-principle-style global count supplies the exhaustive total; equality closes the off-line completeness gap. Once that equality is the proof target, a computation may retain certified sign-change counts without refining and storing every zero ordinate.
historical_or_program_relation: The early Hutchinson-Backlund pattern of matching located witnesses to a rectangle-wide count is the same certificate architecture later made scalable by count-only verification: algorithmic savings come from discarding location detail that the final count comparison does not use.
limits: Sign changes alone are not exhaustive, and the count-only unit does not itself contain its surrounding global completeness proof. The conclusion remains bounded by the certified height or rectangle, and none of these units turns finite agreement into RH at all heights.

title: An error envelope turns uncertain samples into an adaptive evaluation policy
claim: A computed Hardy-Z value yields a rigorous sign only when its magnitude exceeds a method-specific absolute-error envelope. This inequality naturally triages the computation: certify large-margin samples cheaply, and route small-margin cases to slower evaluation or shifted sampling, while recording that shifting changes the measurement protocol and subsequent aggregation.
historical_or_program_relation: Lehmer's SWAC-era remainder-aware screening anticipates later range computations that budget interpolation, analytic truncation, and machine arithmetic separately; later shifted-point runs make explicit that numerical stabilization also creates a bookkeeping confound.
limits: The cited error bounds are tied to particular formulas, machines, and height ranges. Shifted evaluation is not an independent implementation, a stable-looking sign is not a rigorous sign without its bound, and certified sample signs do not by themselves certify that all zeros were counted.

title: Riemann-Siegel speedups form a ladder from analytic compression to certified arithmetic
claim: Choosing the Riemann-Siegel saddle scale reduces a critical-line evaluation to a square-root-length cosine sum with correction terms; precomputed Taylor tables can make those corrections cheap across repeated calls. For the fast representation to support proof, its series truncation, interpolation, coefficient truncation, and floating-point or interval errors must still be converted into a conservative sign margin.
historical_or_program_relation: The computational program progresses by moving work from runtime into analytic specialization and symbolic preprocessing, then by restoring epistemic control through explicit method-specific error accounting; rigorous multiprecision therefore changes both throughput and what the output certifies.
limits: The Taylor-table unit does not provide a uniform bound for its coefficient cutoff, and the later error envelopes apply to their stated implementations rather than automatically validating Pugh's tables. Cross-machine or GHz-hour rates are not comparable without accounting for sampling density, hardware, precision, and rigor.

title: Batch throughput and single-point latency are different optimization targets
claim: An FFT-based method can accelerate a long batch without improving the latency of one adaptively requested Z evaluation, while a processed-height-per-GHz-hour metric can hide the number of samples, precision, and proof obligations per unit height. Computational design must therefore match the cost metric to contiguous verification or sparse exception resolution.
historical_or_program_relation: Large verification campaigns favor amortized batch transforms, whereas exception-driven searches expose the remaining cost of an individual Dirichlet sum; the later rigorous-computation comparison shows why hardware-normalized throughput still does not erase this objective split.
limits: The units do not provide a controlled head-to-head benchmark or select a universally superior algorithm. The conclusion concerns optimization objectives, not mathematical correctness, and any proposed low-latency approximation would still need to fit the existing analytic error budget.

title: A cancellation heuristic becomes useful only after a global-interaction certificate
claim: Near-cancellation in a critical-line evaluation can guide a targeted search toward an unusually close zero pair, but raw closeness is only discovery evidence. After rescaling ordinates into the heat-family coordinates, separately rounded bounds for the pair's surrounding zero interactions must compose into the scalar Lehmer inequality before the pair has dynamical significance.
historical_or_program_relation: Lehmer's recurrence-guided proposal to inspect remote stress regions develops into a discovery-to-certificate loop: broad computation finds a candidate, high precision is concentrated in its window, and analytic local, intermediate, and tail bounds qualify it for a de Bruijn-Newman lower bound.
limits: Recurrence of a cancellation pattern is not recurrence of RH counterexamples, the targeted window is not an exhaustive optimum search, and the certificate concerns the selected pair and a lower bound for Lambda rather than RH or the global distribution of close gaps.

title: A close gap is dynamically meaningful only relative to the other zeros
claim: The Lehmer-pair criterion refuses to treat an adjacent gap in isolation: its static certificate normalizes the gap by an interaction term involving the remaining zeros. Heat-flow analysis supplies the dynamical counterpart, an inverse-distance evolution in which every real zero moves under the surrounding configuration; only after the environmental term is uniformly controlled can a vanishing-gap sequence drive phase-boundary bounds toward zero.
historical_or_program_relation: Pair-based lower bounds turn exceptional static configurations into finite instability certificates, while the later interacting-particle reframing explains why gap relaxation and near-lattice behavior are inherently nonlocal rather than properties of two ordinates alone.
limits: The static Lehmer criterion and the heat-flow ODE are distinct results, and this relation does not derive either from the other. The particle relaxation and unrenormalized Hamiltonian discussion is heuristic at this stage, while the infinite-pair conclusion is conditional on an infinite sequence of certified pairs with the required controlled parameters.

title: Finite computations constrain Lambda through two logically opposite interfaces
claim: A verified-height RH computation becomes an upper bound for the de Bruijn-Newman constant only through a threshold theorem, whereas a certified close-pair configuration becomes a lower bound through a pair-specific instability formula. The phase boundary therefore accepts two different computational inputs with opposite inequality directions: exhaustive coverage below a height and an exceptional local witness.
historical_or_program_relation: Extending zero verification improves a globally transferred upper bound, while searching later ranges for stronger certified gaps improves lower bounds; together they turn computation from undirected RH evidence into two theorem-mediated boundary-measurement programs.
limits: The inputs, transfer theorems, and inequality directions must not be conflated. The stated verified height licenses Lambda at most 0.2 but not the next threshold or RH, and any finite close-pair result supplies only its stated lower bound; neither computation alone pins the boundary at zero.

title: Root counting replaces root location with opposite logical polarity in two programs
claim: Both finite RH verification and the Jensen-polynomial obstruction search avoid approximating every complex root, but their count logic is dual. For zeta, an on-line witness count matching an independent total excludes additional off-line zeros in a bounded region; for a Jensen polynomial, a complete real-root count below the degree establishes that some roots are nonreal and hence supplies an existential obstruction.
historical_or_program_relation: The older contour-count-plus-sign-change architecture and the later Sturm-chain computation share a decision-oriented compression of root data, yet one proves absence by equality while the other proves existence by deficit.
limits: A Sturm theorem for exact coefficients is distinct from floating-point Sturm-sign evaluation, so interval coverage and sign stability remain separate obligations. The zeta count is analytic and region-bounded, the Jensen count is algebraic and polynomial-specific, and the analogy transfers certificate logic rather than either theorem's hypotheses.

title: Cheap computational surrogates must be reranked against the downstream objective
claim: Landau's inexpensive polynomial score can rank candidates differently from the full finite zero-free-region constant, just as an outer-first Gram-block search policy tuned to common short blocks loses efficiency on rare long blocks. In both cases, the cheap stage should generate or order candidates, while task-specific evaluation or a conditional branch determines the final choice.
historical_or_program_relation: The zero-free-region search retains diverse near-optimal surrogate polynomials and reruns the expensive R0 calculation; the zero-verification search uses empirical block type and length to identify where a once-effective query order should branch. Both are corrections to optimizing a proxy as though its ranking were invariant.
limits: This is a shared computational-design relation, not a claim that polynomial optimization and zero search have the same mathematics. Neither source proves a global optimizer: the polynomial pool is finite and expanded heuristically, while the Gram-block distributions and strategy crossover are empirical and range-dependent.
